Applicability and utility The final guideline will be disseminated by publication in the journal Rheumatology (Oxford) and will be freely available on the BSR website. It is recognized that constraints within the healthcare system may create challenges to widespread implementation of this guideline. For instance, many centres do not have access to minor salivary gland biopsy and not all have access to expert salivary gland USS. Access to certain treatments, e.g. serum eye drops are limited by cost and availability and there are currently no immunomodulatory treatments licensed for use in SD. Most of the immunosuppressive drugs are used off-licence for this indication. Biologics are not NICE approved for SD. Of the few patients who do get biologics this is usually either as part of a clinical trial or because they meet criteria for RA or another CTD (usually SLE). Research recommendations There are significant unmet needs in the management of this patient cohort. Further research into pathogenetic mechanisms may facilitate the development of targeted treatments. Accurate stratification of patients into disease subgroups and collaborative studies are essential to provide large enough cohorts to demonstrate meaningful effects of interventions. There is a need to develop better measures of disease activity as the currently used parameters do not include fatigue and dryness, underestimate the disease burden and are not sensitive to change. There is also a need to develop Quality Standards for SD to improve standards of care. Audit A model audit tool is available via the BSR website and in available at Rheumatology online. We would also strongly recommend that new cases of SD are recorded in the NEIAA (New Early Inflammatory Arthritis Audit https://arthritisaudit.org.uk/ ) database to provide information on the incidence and demographics of the condition plus collect evidence on diagnostic delays and route of referral. Conclusions SD remains an under-recognized condition with significant unmet needs. Nonetheless, we do feel that following these guidelines will provide a framework for health professionals to manage those with SD effectively and proactively. There are a number of studies underway investigating non-pharmacological treatments, novel biologic drugs and repurposing of existing conventional and biologic immunosuppressive agents. The NEIAA has recently expanded to include new CTD diagnosis, including SD, and we would encourage teams to record all newly diagnosed cases. Supplementary Material keae152_Supplementary_Data

chunks.content: Introduction Gout is the most common cause of inflammatory arthritis, especially in Western countries, and its prevalence is increasing. This is despite the long-term availability of effective therapies and largely consistent management guidelines. Gout results from sustained high levels of uric acid leading to crystal deposition and acute arthritis in genetically susceptible people. Outcomes of this include tophi, chronic arthritis, kidney stones and renal impairment, as well as, most commonly, recurrent acute arthritis. Gout is also frequently associated with comorbidities such as metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease as well as premature mortality. Risk factors for hyperuricemia and gout are well understood and include age, male gender, alcohol consumption, postmenopausal status in females, renal impairment, diuretic therapy, and genetic control of urate transport, as well as a number of drugs. Reasons for why gout is poorly controlled include poor compliance with potentially curative medication, especially by males, and suboptimal use of existing therapies. In the last decade, more options have become available, and this has resulted in a plethora of new guidelines. , , The aim of this review is to describe the role of combination therapy in gout, with a focus on a new therapeutic agent named lesinurad (LESU). In general, there is consensus that the target urate level is 6 mg/dL or less for acute gout and 5 mg/dL or less for chronic or tophaceous gout. , , Most guidelines focus on lifestyle modification and monotherapy with allopurinol (APL) or febuxostat (FBX) as standard of care. All the recent guidelines make a comment about combination therapy ( ). The American College of Rheumatology and British Society of Rheumatology guidelines say that combination therapy is indicated if serum urate (SUA) target has not been met by appropriate or optimal dosing of a xanthine oxidase inhibitor. In comparison, the European League against Rheumatism states that uricosuric monotherapy, FBX monotherapy, or combination therapy are all reasonable options if APL monotherapy fails. The guidelines are relatively silent on what is an optimal dose of APL monotherapy. Renal function and, potentially, urinary urate excretion should be assessed prior to starting therapy. Most clinicians use a dose of up to 300 mg/d with a dose adjustment for renal impairment, and they are reticent about higher dose rates. Emerging evidence suggests this caution is not warranted. shows success rates for various approaches to gout therapy. There are few head-to-head studies but these studies do have similar inclusion criteria. It is apparent that the usual dose of APL is not that successful even in the setting of controlled trials, with only 30%–70% achieving target SUA. In a real-world setting, this is likely to be worse given the poor compliance with therapy. If one pushes the APL dose to 600 mg/d, then success rates are considerably better, with 69%–78% achieving a target SUA. , Some rheumatologists use even higher doses up to 1,200 mg/d, but there is no published evidence to support this practice. APL is cheap and has a well-known safety profile. Serious side effects are rare but include hypersensitivity syndromes such as Stevens–Johnson Syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. These may be more common in those with renal impairment, short duration of therapy, concomitant diuretic use, and HLA-B*5801 type. In our opinion, increasing the dose seems a very logical step if target SUA is not achieved. There is good evidence that the dose of APL needed to achieve target concentrations of urate is a function of the baseline serum urate concentration, with higher concentrations needing higher doses. FBX is another xanthine oxidase inhibitor. In both indirect and direct comparisons, it appears considerably more effective than APL at achieving a target SUA, especially at 80 mg/d, indicating it provides stronger blockade of xanthine oxidase ( ). In a number of jurisdictions, it can be used first line, but in some countries such as Australia it is only approved for those who fail APL either for efficacy or toxicity (due to its higher cost). Uricosurics There are a number of uricosuric agents which increase uric acid excretion in the urine. These include sulfinpyrazone, probenecid, benzbromarone, fenofibrate, losartan, and high-dose aspirin. These agents are not available in all jurisdictions, eg, Australia only has probenecid. In clinical practice, they are most commonly used in combination. Data for existing medications is summarized in . There is very limited controlled data. Both benzbromarone and probenecid in combination are more effective than APL monotherapy based on three small trials. No controlled data is available on the other agents. LESU LESU is a new selective uric acid reabsorption inhibitor that has recently been given US Food and Drug Administration and European Medicines Agency approval and marketing authorization. While mentioned in the British Society of Rheumatology guidelines, no recommendations for its use were given. This review will summarize the four key clinical trials. – provides the summary efficacy data for comparison purposes. provides safety data. APL in combination with LESU The initial Phase II trial evaluated the efficacy and tolerability of LESU in combination with APL versus APL monotherapy in patients with active gout and an inadequate response to APL (defined as an SUA consistently ≥6 mg/d). The patients were randomized 2:1 to 4 weeks of double-blind treatment with LESU (200, 400 or 600 mg/d) or matching placebo (PBO) in combination with their APL dose at study entry (200–600 mg/d). Colchicine prophylaxis for gout flares was given to all patients. The primary endpoint was change in SUA levels at 4 weeks. A pharmacokinetic substudy was also conducted. Safety was assessed throughout. Patients (n=208) received ≥1 dose of blinded medication. LESU 200, 400, and 600 mg in combination with APL produced significant mean percent reductions from baseline SUA of 16%, 22%, and 30%, respectively, versus a mean 3% increase with PBO ( p <0.0001, all doses versus PBO). Similar results were observed in patients with an estimated creatinine clearance down to 30 mL/min. The incidence of adverse events was 46%, 48%, and 54% with LESU 200, 400, and 600 mg, respectively, and 46% with PBO, with no deaths or serious adverse events. The authors concluded that LESU achieves important reductions in SUA in combination with APL in patients who warrant additional therapy on APL alone. The CLEAR 1 study was a 12-month, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, PBO-controlled Phase III trial conducted to evaluate daily LESU (200 mg or 400 mg orally) added to APL versus PBO plus APL in patients with SUA levels above 6.5 mg/dL and in whom active gout during the previous year was studied. The primary endpoint was the percentage of patients achieving an SUA <6.0 mg/dL at month 6. Key secondary endpoints were the mean gout flare rate requiring treatment (months 7–12) and the proportions of patients with complete resolution of at least 1 target tophus (month 12). The study patients (n=603) were predominantly male with a mean age of 51.9 years, gout duration of 11.8 years, and baseline SUA level of 6.94 mg/dL, and they were receiving an APL dosage of just over 300 mg/d. LESU at doses of 200 mg or 400 mg added to APL therapy significantly increased the proportions of patients who achieved SUA target levels by month 6 as compared with those receiving APL monotherapy (54.2%, 59.2%, and 27.9%, respectively, p <0.0001). LESU was not significantly superior to APL alone for rates of gout flares and resolution of tophi. LESU was generally well tolerated except for higher rates of predominantly reversible renal impairment ( ). The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infections, sinusitis, increased blood creatinine levels, and headache. Serious adverse events apart from renal complications included cerebrovascular accidents (two patients), coronary artery disease (two patients), congestive heart failure (two patients), and acute myocardial infarction (three patients). The authors concluded that LESU added to APL was better than APL alone at reducing SUA levels. It would be logical to suggest this should also result in better clinical outcomes, but the study was perhaps too short to demonstrate this. LESU in combination with FBX The initial study was a Phase Ib, multicenter, open-label, multiple-dose study of gout patients with high SUA (>8 mg/dL) following cessation of urate lowering therapy. The aim of this study was to evaluate the pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and safety of LESU in combination with FBX. FBX 40 or 80 mg/d was administered on days 1–21, LESU 400 mg/d was added on days 8–14, and then LESU was increased to 600 mg/d on days 15–21. SUA, urine uric acid, and pharmacokinetic profiles were evaluated at the end of each week. Initial FBX monotherapy resulted in one-half to two-thirds of subjects achieving an SUA level <6 mg/dL. FBX plus LESU 400 or 600 mg/d resulted in virtually all patients achieving a level under 5 mg/dL. No clinically relevant changes in drug pharmacokinetics were observed. However, LESU did increase feboxustat concentrations by a small % and decreased colchicine levels by 20%. An increase in creatine kinase levels was observed. Safety was similar to the other trials. FBX plus LESU 400 or 600 mg/d resulted in virtually all patients achieving a level under 5 mg/dL. No clinically relevant changes in drug pharmacokinetics were observed. However, LESU did increase feboxustat concentrations by a small % and decreased colchicine levels by 20%. An increase in creatine kinase levels was observed. Safety was similar to the other trials. The authors concluded that the clinically important targets of SUA are achievable in 100% of patients with combination therapy. This was then followed by the CRYSTAL study which aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of LESU in combination with FBX in patients with tophaceous gout in a 12-month, Phase III trial. We included patients with high SUA (≥8.0 mg/dL or ≥6.0 mg/dL on preexisting urate-lowering therapy) and at least one tophus who were given FBX 80 mg daily for a run-in period 4 weeks before randomization to LESU (200 or 400 mg daily) or PBO in combination with FBX. The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients achieving SUA <5.0 mg/dL at 6 months, while other endpoints measured tophus size and resolution at 12 months. Patients (N=324) were predominately male with a mean age of 54.1 years. Significantly more patients achieved SUA target levels with the combination of FBX and LESU 400 mg (76.1%; p <0.0001), but not 200 mg (56.6%; p =0.13), versus FBX alone (46.8%). With the exception of the primary timepoint, more patients in the LESU 200 mg group achieved the SUA target. Complete tophus resolution was not different between groups (but this was an ambitious target within the study timeframe). However, LESU (200 mg and 400 mg) plus FBX reduced total target tophi area versus FBX monotherapy (50.1% and 52.9% versus 28.3%, respectively, p <0.05). Safety was generally comparable with FBX alone, except for higher rates of predominately reversible serum creatinine elevation, particularly with LESU 400 mg ( ). The most common adverse events were nasopharyngitis, hypertension, headache, and extremity and back pain. The authors concluded that LESU in combination with FBX demonstrated superior SUA lowering compared with FBX alone with a clinically relevant effect on tophi in patients with tophaceous gout warranting additional therapy. Results with the larger trial appeared to not be as beneficial as the earlier phase trial. In summary, LESU in combination with either APL or FBX is more effective than either agent as monotherapy in well-conducted multicenter trials. There is clear evidence of a dose response for both efficacy and toxicity. The combinations did not resolve tophi within the study timeframes but did decrease tophus area. Both the 200 and 400 mg dose have been approved. LESU can be used with an eGFR as low as 30 mL/min with no apparent change in efficacy. No data is available in any trials in patients with eGFR under 30 mL/min, so use in this group should not be considered at this point in time until more data becomes available. LESU-induced renal impairment is generally mild and often transient, but is common especially at the 400 mg dose. This is thought to be due to urate deposition in the kidney. This should be carefully monitored until longer term studies become available. Similarly, an increase in creatinine kinase is also not uncommon. The mechanism is unclear but may be due to an interaction with or alterations in colchicine metabolism (as this was given as prophylaxis in most of these trials). This usually did not cause symptoms but should be monitored. Place in therapy This review indicates that there are a number of ways to approach patients who do not achieve a target SUA with APL monotherapy. These include higher doses of APL up to 600–800 mg/d, switching to FBX, or using a xanthine oxidase inhibitor in combination with a uricosuric agent. All appear similar in terms of success rates, so which option to use comes down to physician and patient choice, cost, experience, and strength of the evidence base. The strongest evidence for the uricosuric combination option is available for LESU as trials of other agents are either nonexistent or based on small single-centre trials or the medicine is not available in major markets. These authors partly agree with the European League against Rheumatism guidelines, but suggest these should be expanded to consider all evidence-based options in the not-uncommon event of APL inadequate response.

documents.title: BSR guideline on diagnosis and treatment of giant cell arteritis

chunks.content: Highlight key points Initial GC initiation and tapering practices for polymyalgia rheumatica were largely consistent with international guideline recommendations, while considerable variability was observed in diagnostic approaches and screening strategies for giant cell arteritis. The use of imaging modalities, including musculoskeletal ultrasonography, magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography, showed marked heterogeneity among rheumatologists, despite their inclusion in contemporary classification criteria and management guidelines. Gaps between guideline recommendations and real-world practice highlight unmet needs in imaging access, standardized assessment, and follow-up–related management in PMR. Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is a common inflammatory rheumatic condition occurring almost exclusively in adults over 50 years of age and characterized by bilateral shoulder, neck, and hip girdle pain with prominent early morning stiffness, reflecting inflammation of periarticular structures [ ]. In the absence of a disease-specific biomarker, PMR remains a clinical diagnosis of exclusion. Assessment relies on typical symptom patterns, physical examination, and nonspecific laboratory abnormalities [ ]. Although the 2012 European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology (EULAR/ACR) provisional criteria [ ] provide a standardized framework, they were designed primarily for research settings, limiting their diagnostic utility in routine care. Furthermore, despite evidence that shoulder and hip ultrasonography (US) improves diagnostic accuracy, its uptake remains inconsistent across centers. Diagnostic uncertainty has also been demonstrated in primary care. In a large UK multi-methods study, general practitioners frequently reported difficulty distinguishing PMR from mimicking conditions and often relied on glucocorticoid (GC) responsiveness to support the diagnosis [ ]. Recommended investigations to exclude alternative inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic disorders were inconsistently performed, and concerns regarding long-term GC monitoring were widespread [ ]. As this work focused exclusively on primary care, it did not capture specialist-level decision-making. Complementary evidence from a multinational survey involving general practitioners (n=394) and rheumatologists (n=937) revealed substantial heterogeneity in referral pathways, timing of specialist assessment, initial GC dosing, and imaging practices, with many patients already started on prednisolone before rheumatology evaluation [ ]. Together, these observations indicate that variability in PMR management arises at multiple levels of care. This reliance on clinical judgment may contribute to variability in diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making in PMR. Despite the availability of structured management algorithms in international guidelines, including the 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations and the 2010 British Society for Rheumatology/British Health Professionals in Rheumatology (BSR/BHPR) guideline [ , ], real-world practice remains heterogeneous, particularly with regard to initial GC dosing, tapering strategies, and the use of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). Clinical overlap between PMR and giant cell arteritis (GCA) is well recognized: approximately half of individuals with GCA develop polymyalgic symptoms during the disease course, and nearly one-fifth carry a prior PMR diagnosis [ ]. Despite increasing recognition of subclinical GCA, contemporary guidelines provide limited guidance on this issue. Both the 2024 BSR guideline scope [ ] and the 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations [ ] explicitly exclude concomitant or suspected GCA from their remit, offering no standardized approach to vascular imaging in PMR. This gap is particularly relevant given the increasing use of imaging modalities such as US and positron emission tomography (PET) in selected settings. In routine practice, screening for subclinical vasculitis remains uncommon and is generally limited to patients with suggestive clinical features [ ]. Unrecognized vasculitis has been proposed to contribute to higher initial GC requirements and more gradual tapering strategies, raising questions regarding the potential role of baseline vascular imaging in PMR [ ]. Consequently, approaches to GCA screening vary widely among rheumatologists, reflecting the absence of unified guidance and further contributing to heterogeneity in real-world practice. In Turkiye, the absence of national PMR guidelines, variability in postgraduate rheumatology training, and structural differences in access to imaging and referral pathways between secondary and tertiary care settings are likely to further contextualize this variability within the Turkish healthcare system. Although international rheumatology guidelines have gained substantial academic prominence in recent decades [ ], evidence on their consistent implementation in routine clinical practice, particularly across different healthcare settings, remains limited. To date, no nationwide study has evaluated how Turkish rheumatologists interpret and implement international PMR guidelines. Therefore, this survey aimed to describe real-world diagnostic and management practices for PMR in Turkiye including approaches to imaging and screening for GCA and to compare these practices with contemporary international guideline recommendations. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study Design and Participants This nationwide, cross-sectional survey was conducted among rheumatologists currently practicing in Turkiye, including rheumatology fellows in training and practicing specialists. Data were collected using a self-administered online questionnaire disseminated through professional communication networks between 15 September and 20 October 2025. Participation was voluntary, and completion of the questionnaire was considered to indicate implied informed consent. Responses were collected and analyzed in a de-identified manner. As the survey was distributed through professional networks, the total number of rheumatologists who received or viewed the invitation could not be determined, and a response rate could therefore not be calculated. No formal a priori sample size calculation was performed, and all responses received during the survey period were included in the final analysis. Survey Instrument The questionnaire was developed with reference to the 2012 EULAR/ACR classification criteria [ ] and international management guidelines, including the 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations [ ] and the 2010 BSR/BHPR guideline [ ]. It was administered electronically as a self-completed online survey using Google Forms® (Google LLC, Mountain View, CA, USA). Draft versions were reviewed by senior rheumatologists to ensure clarity, face validity, and clinical relevance before dissemination. The final survey contained 29 items structured into the following domains: Demographics and professional profile (Q1–6): Gender, age, years in rheumatology practice, academic rank, institution type, and geographic region. PMR case volume (Q7): Number of patients diagnosed with PMR in the past 6 months. Diagnostic approach (Q8–16): Use of classification/diagnostic criteria, reliance on erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and/or C-reactive protein (CRP), imaging preferences including US, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and PET, and screening for GCA. Treatment preferences (Q17–20): Initial therapeutic choices (GC alone or in combination with DMARDs), use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), preferred initial GC starting dose, and tapering strategy. Follow-up and monitoring practices (Q21–27): Criteria for initiating DMARD therapy, relapse management, referral for individualized exercise programs, assessment of osteoporosis and fracture risk, and use of dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) and the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX). Barriers to guideline adherence (Q28): Main obstacles to full adherence to PMR management guidelines. Open-ended item (Q29, optional): Main challenges encountered in PMR management. The survey was designed with reference to the Checklist for Reporting Results of Internet E-Surveys (CHERRIES) guidelines and reported accordingly [ ]. The full survey questionnaire is provided in . Appendix 1 Ethics Approval The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Goztepe Prof. Dr. Suleyman Yalcin City Hospital (Approval No: 2025/0112; Date: 11 September 2025). This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments. Statistical Analysis Survey responses were exported to Microsoft Excel and analyzed using SPSS software (version 25.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Categorical variables were reported as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were summarized as means with standard deviations (SD) or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), as appropriate. The primary analyses were descriptive. Exploratory analyses were limited to trend assessment between years of clinical experience and selected practice patterns using linear-by-linear association, where applicable. A two-tailed p value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS A total of 101 rheumatologists completed the survey. The cohort was predominantly female (71, 70.3%), with most participants falling within the 31–40-year age group (67, 66.3%). Nearly half of the participants reported 5–10 years of clinical experience in rheumatology (50, 49.5%), whereas only a minority had more than 20 years in practice (4, 4.0%). Specialists represented the largest professional subgroup (52, 51.5%), followed by associate professors (23, 22.8%) and fellows (14, 13.9%). Participants were employed across a range of healthcare settings; city hospitals were the most common workplace (32, 31.7%), while university hospitals and training and research hospitals each accounted for 24 participants (23.8%). Representation was obtained from all geographic regions of Turkiye, with the highest proportion originating from the Marmara region (39, 38.6%), followed by Central Anatolia (27, 26.7%). A comprehensive summary of the demographic and professional characteristics of the study population is provided in . The majority of participants reported diagnosing five or fewer patients with PMR in the preceding six months, and no statistically significant differences were observed in PMR case numbers across the geographic regions of Turkiye. Regarding diagnostic resources, use of the 2012 EULAR/ACR provisional classification criteria was reported by 65 (64.4%), referral to the BSR/BHPR guidelines by 10 (9.9%), and primary reliance on clinical judgment by 76 (75.2%). The diagnostic approach did not differ significantly across levels of professional experience. PET imaging was requested most frequently in cases of suspected malignancy by 70 participants (69.3%), followed by suspected GCA by 55 participants (54.5%) and steroid-resistant disease by 40 participants (39.6%). No statistically significant differences were observed within this sample between healthcare institutions in the use or ordering of imaging modalities. Screening for GCA only in the presence of suggestive clinical signs or symptoms was reported by 76 participants (75.2%), whereas routine GCA screening in all patients with suspected PMR was reported by 25 (24.8%). GC monotherapy was the preferred first-line treatment in 76 participants (75.2%). An initial GC dose of 12.5–25 mg/day (prednisolone equivalent) was selected by 73 (72.3%), and 55 (54.5%) reported beginning tapering between weeks 4 and 8. More than half of the participants (55, 54.5%) initiated DMARD therapy at the first relapse. As shown in , increasing the GC dose (87, 86.1%) and adding a DMARD (85, 84.2%) were the most frequently used strategies for relapse management, while smaller proportions used tocilizumab (30, 29.7%), requested imaging (30, 29.7%), or screened for GCA (44, 43.6%). Approximately half of the participants reported that their patients had been receiving treatment for 1–2 years, 51 participants (50.5%), while 43 (42.6%) indicated treatment duration longer than 2 years and 7 (6.9%) reported durations shorter than 1 year. The most frequently reported barrier to guideline adherence was patient non-adherence, reported by 36 participants (35.6%), followed by concerns regarding treatment side effects (31, 30.7%), time constraints in clinical practice (25, 24.8%), limited access to guideline-recommended medications (7, 6.9%), and patient comorbidities (2, 2.0%). A total of 86 participants (85.1%) reported routinely evaluating patients diagnosed with PMR for osteoporosis and fracture risk, and 53 (52.5%) reported ordering DXA. Additionally, 79 participants (78.2%) stated that they did not routinely refer patients for personalized exercise planning or calculate FRAX scores. There were no significant differences between healthcare institutions regarding DXA requests, FRAX score calculation, or referrals for exercise planning. Themes identified from the open-ended question (answered by 39 participants) were derived through descriptive categorization rather than formal qualitative analysis. Concerns about side effects and comorbidities were reported most frequently (16, 41.0%), followed by patient non-adherence issues (14, 35.9%). Additional challenges included issues related to insurance coverage for medications and institutional limitations (7, 17.9%), difficulties in differential diagnosis (5, 12.8%), lack of specific markers reflecting disease activity (2, 5.1%), and challenges in managing relapses (1, 2.6%). DISCUSSION To our knowledge, this is a nationwide evaluation of real-world diagnostic and therapeutic practices for PMR among rheumatologists in Turkiye. Our findings show substantial heterogeneity across key aspects of care: only 64.4% reported using the 2012 EULAR/ACR criteria, 24.8% routinely screened for GCA, and recommended osteoporosis assessments such as DXA and FRAX were performed by 52.5% and 21.8% of clinicians, respectively. In contrast, GC monotherapy and guideline-consistent starting doses (12.5–25 mg/day in 72.3%) were widely adopted, highlighting a gap between diagnostic/monitoring recommendations and routine practice. The low PMR case volumes reported by rheumatologists in our survey are consistent with previous epidemiologic data from Turkiye [ ]. In a population-based study from northwestern Turkiye, the annual incidence rates for GCA and PMR in individuals aged ≥50 years were 1.13/100,000 and 3.15/100,000, respectively [ ] markedly lower than Scandinavian rates, where incidence exceeds 20/100,000 and prevalences reach 68.3/100,000 in Denmark [ ] and 50/100,000 in Sweden [ ]. These patterns may reflect experience-related variation, combined with the absence of a diagnostic gold standard in PMR, influencing how consistently clinicians use guideline-based tools. It should be emphasized that the 2012 EULAR/ACR criteria were developed as classification criteria rather than diagnostic criteria [ ]. Their primary purpose is to standardize patient selection for research, not to establish a definitive diagnosis in individual patients. In routine clinical practice, clinicians often integrate these classification frameworks with comprehensive clinical judgment, longitudinal follow-up, and treatment response. This distinction is particularly relevant in PMR, where no disease-specific diagnostic biomarker exists, and may partly explain the variable reliance on the 2012 EULAR/ACR criteria observed in our survey. Diagnostic uncertainty may also stem from atypical presentations. A Turkish study found normal ESR and CRP values in 14% of clinically diagnosed PMR patients [ ], demonstrating that inflammatory markers are not invariably elevated. Nonetheless, ESR and/or CRP remain central to routine diagnostic reasoning and the 2012 EULAR/ACR classification criteria [ ]. In line with this, 91.1% of participants in our survey required at least one elevated acute-phase reactant for diagnosis. Even in the validation cohort of the 2012 EULAR/ACR criteria, the final diagnosis changed in 7.8% of patients [ ], underscoring the limitations of relying on clinical judgment alone without supportive imaging or longitudinal assessment. Accordingly, imaging is recommended in situations such as atypical presentations, normal inflammatory markers, inadequate GC response, suspected large-vessel GCA, or high risk of GC toxicity [ ]. In our survey, imaging practices showed considerable variation. US, MRI, and particularly PET scans were used inconsistently; PET was requested most commonly when malignancy was suspected, followed by suspected GCA and steroid-resistant disease. Screening strategies for GCA also varied widely. Differences in GCA screening approaches among Turkish rheumatologists may be influenced by local contextual factors. The absence of national PMR guidelines in Turkiye, heterogeneity in access to vascular and musculoskeletal imaging across institutions, variability in clinical service delivery between tertiary centers and peripheral hospitals, and differences in clinicians’ experience may collectively shape these practices. Such system-level disparities may help explain why substantial variation persists, even when international recommendations are uniform. Initial treatment practices in our cohort were largely aligned with international guideline recommendations [ , ]. GC monotherapy was preferred by 75.2% of clinicians, with most selecting a starting dose within the recommended 12.5–25 mg/day range and initiating tapering between weeks 4 and 8, consistent with both the 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations and the 2010 BSR/BHPR guideline [ , ]. In contrast, relapse management demonstrated greater variability: increasing GC doses (86.1%) and adding a DMARD (84.2%) were the most commonly adopted strategies, while tocilizumab was used less frequently (29.7%). This pattern reflects current guidance, which conditionally recommends early methotrexate (MTX) in patients at high risk of relapse or prolonged GC exposure and reserves biologic therapy for refractory disease [ ]. In this context, the limited use of tocilizumab and the absence of TNF inhibitors appear appropriate and may reflect a cautious, stepwise approach to biologic therapy, particularly in healthcare settings without nationally endorsed PMR guidelines. Observational studies indicate that prolonged GC exposure is common in PMR: up to 85% of patients experience GC-related adverse events, half remain on treatment after 2 years, and one-quarter continue beyond 5 years [ , ]. Our survey showed similar patterns, with 50.5% of clinicians treating patients for 1–2 years and 42.6% for more than 2 years. Despite guideline emphasis on minimizing GC duration [ ], prolonged courses remain common, underscoring real-world challenges in tapering. The 2015 EULAR/ACR recommendations also emphasize patient education, fracture prevention, and referral for individually tailored exercise programs [ ]. Although most clinicians (85.1%) reported routinely evaluating osteoporosis risk, implementation gaps were evident: only 52.5% ordered DXA, and the majority did not calculate FRAX scores or refer patients for exercise planning. Limited access to allied health services, time constraints, or uncertainty regarding benefit may contribute to this discrepancy. The challenges reported by participants including concerns about GC toxicity, patient non-adherence, system-level obstacles, diagnostic uncertainty, and difficulties in managing relapses—closely mirror observations from other healthcare settings. In a large UK multi-methods study, general practitioners similarly described diagnostic uncertainty, frequent reliance on GC responsiveness, and inconsistent investigation of alternative diagnoses, along with widespread concerns about long-term GC adverse effects and variable monitoring practices [ ]. These international parallels indicate that the difficulties identified in our survey are not unique to Turkiye but rather reflect broader, system-level challenges inherent to PMR management. This study has several strengths. It provides nationwide representation by including rheumatologists from all major regions of Turkiye, offering a comprehensive overview of specialist-level PMR management. Unlike prior studies focused on primary care, this survey specifically reflects the practices of rheumatologists, who are primarily responsible for diagnostic evaluation, longitudinal monitoring, and treatment escalation. The questionnaire captured multiple domains—including diagnostic criteria use, imaging strategies, GCA assessment, GC dosing and tapering, relapse management, and osteoporosis prevention—allowing a multidimensional evaluation of real-world practice patterns across different levels of clinical seniority. Nevertheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. The cross-sectional, self-reported design carries risks of recall and social desirability bias, and voluntary participation may have introduced selection bias. As the survey was disseminated through professional communication networks, the total number of rheumatologists who received or viewed the invitation could not be determined, precluding calculation of a formal response rate and limiting full assessment of sample representativeness. Moreover, because the data reflect self-reported practice patterns rather than audited patient-level records, the findings indicate perceived concordance with guideline recommendations rather than objectively measured adherence. The absence of patient-level clinical data further restricts the ability to link reported management strategies with actual outcomes. Future research should therefore focus on prospective, patient-level studies evaluating diagnostic pathways, imaging strategies, and longitudinal outcomes, including GC exposure, relapse rates, and treatment-related adverse events. Mixed-methods approaches incorporating qualitative interviews may also help elucidate system-level and behavioral barriers to guideline implementation. Conclusion This nationwide survey provides a comprehensive assessment of specialist-level PMR management in Turkiye and demonstrates marked variability across key domains of care. Although initial GC treatment was largely aligned with international guideline recommendations, substantial inconsistencies were observed in the use of classification criteria, imaging modalities, screening strategies for GCA, and follow-up–related management. These findings underscore persistent gaps between guideline recommendations and real-world clinical practice, likely reflecting the absence of a diagnostic gold standard, heterogeneity in clinical experience, and structural constraints within the healthcare system. Overall, our results highlight the need for more standardized and context-sensitive approaches to PMR care in Turkiye.
